definition:
Justification is God's verdict. To justify, in the Bible's sense, is not to make excuses for someone or to explain why they did what they did; it is to declare, as a judge declares in court, that a person stands in the right. The doctrine answers the oldest question of religion, which Job asked in a single line: “how can a mortal be righteous before God?” (Job 9:2). The New Testament's answer, set out most fully by Paul in Galatians and Romans, is that sinners who cannot acquit themselves are acquitted by God as a gift, “justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 3:24), and that this verdict is received through faith in Christ, not earned by keeping the law. The verdict brings peace with God now and anticipates the last judgment, so that the believer can already say, “there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Justification is one part of the larger rescue the Bible calls salvation; its neighbors, union with Christ and sanctification, have their own studies.

The vocabulary is legal from the start. The Hebrew root is tsadaq, ‘to be in the right’, with the nouns tsedeq and tsedaqah, ‘righteousness’ or ‘justice’. In its causative form (hitsdiq) the verb means ‘to declare in the right’ or ‘to acquit’, the word a judge uses when he rules for the innocent party (Deuteronomy 25:1). The Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint (the translation of the Hebrew Scriptures made by Jews in Egypt from the third century BC), rendered this with dikaioō, the verb the New Testament uses about thirty-nine times, most of them in Paul. Its family includes dikaios, ‘righteous’ or ‘just’, dikaiosynē, ‘righteousness’ or ‘justice’, and dikaiōsis, ‘justification’ or ‘acquittal’ (Romans 4:25; 5:18). English needs two word families, ‘just’ and ‘righteous’, for what Greek says with one, which is why ‘justify’ and ‘righteousness’ look unrelated in English Bibles when they are the same idea. A second key word is the verb ‘credit’ or ‘reckon’, Hebrew chashab and Greek logizomai, used of Abraham's faith being counted as righteousness (Genesis 15:6; Romans 4:3-8).
ot:
The Old Testament lays the ground in three ways: it shows what a just verdict is, it shows that no one can claim one before God on his own record, and it shows God promising to put his people in the right himself. Righteousness in the Hebrew Bible is not an abstract moral quality so much as rightness within a relationship, measured by a standard. When Judah, confronted with his own injustice, says of Tamar, “She is more righteous than I” (Genesis 38:26), he means she was in the right and he in the wrong. The law of Moses charges Israel's judges to acquit the innocent and condemn the guilty (Deuteronomy 25:1), and God himself says, “I will not acquit the guilty” (Exodus 23:7). Proverbs calls the reverse, “Acquitting the guilty and condemning the righteous”, detestable to the LORD (Proverbs 17:15), and Isaiah condemns judges “who acquit the guilty for a bribe” (Isaiah 5:23). These texts matter because they set the problem Paul will face: if God is a just judge, how can he acquit the ungodly without becoming the kind of judge his own law condemns.

The first word of the answer comes early. When Abram, old and childless, is shown the stars and promised offspring beyond counting, “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). The verse comes before the covenant of circumcision in Genesis 17 and centuries before Sinai, a sequence Paul later presses hard (Romans 4:9-12). The same language is used of Phinehas, whose zeal “was credited to him as righteousness for endless generations to come” (Psalm 106:31), and Jewish interpreters in the Second Temple period (the centuries between the return from exile and the destruction of the temple in AD 70) often read Genesis 15:6 alongside that text, as describing faithfulness God rewards. Paul reads Genesis 15 differently, as God counting as righteous a man whose only contribution was trust in a promise.

The Psalms and the Prophets deepen both sides. On one side, “no one alive is righteous before You” (Psalm 143:2), and “If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand?” (Psalm 130:3). On the other, David speaks of the man “whose iniquity the LORD does not count against him” (Psalm 32:2), the very language of crediting turned inside out, and Paul quotes the psalm for exactly that reason (Romans 4:6-8). In Solomon's prayer at the temple the king asks God to judge between his servants, “justifying the righteous man by rewarding him according to his righteousness” (1 Kings 8:32), the ordinary court sense. The prophets then speak of God's own righteousness as his saving action for his people. Isaiah hears the promise, “In the LORD all descendants of Israel will be justified and will exult” (Isaiah 45:25), and the Servant of the LORD, the figure of Isaiah 52 and 53 who suffers for the sins of others, is the one of whom God says, “By His knowledge My righteous Servant will justify many, and He will bear their iniquities” (Isaiah 53:11). The verdict and the bearing of iniquity stand side by side in one verse. Jeremiah promises a king from David's line whose name is “The LORD Our Righteousness” (Jeremiah 23:6).

Two more scenes complete the ground. Zechariah sees Joshua the high priest standing in filthy garments before the angel of the LORD while Satan, whose name means ‘the accuser’, stands ready to accuse him; God rebukes the accuser, and the angel says, “See, I have removed your iniquity, and I will clothe you with splendid robes” (Zechariah 3:4). Isaiah's redeemed people sing that God “has clothed me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in a robe of righteousness” (Isaiah 61:10). And Habakkuk, waiting through the Babylonian crisis near the end of the seventh century BC, receives the line that Paul will make a banner: “the righteous will live by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4). The Hebrew word there, 'emunah, means steadiness or faithfulness; the Septuagint rendered it with pistis, which can mean both faith and faithfulness. Scholars discuss whether Paul reads the verse as the believer's faith, as God's faithfulness, or, some argue, as a messianic reference to the Righteous One, and all agree that for Habakkuk it described the one who keeps trusting God when the promise is delayed. At Qumran, the community of the Dead Sea Scrolls, the closing hymn of the Community Rule (1QS 10-11) confesses that the worshiper's justification rests on God's righteousness and mercy, not his own, and the halakhic letter 4QMMT speaks of certain ‘works of the law’ being reckoned as righteousness, the nearest known parallel to Paul's phrase.
nt:
Jesus uses the courtroom language sparingly but pointedly. He tells of a Pharisee (a member of a devout movement known for careful keeping of the law) and a tax collector praying in the temple; the tax collector, unable to lift his eyes, asks only for mercy, and Jesus says, “this man, rather than the Pharisee, went home justified” (Luke 18:14). He warns the Pharisees, “You are the ones who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts” (Luke 16:15), and a lawyer in Luke 10:29 asks who his neighbor is because he wants to justify himself. The verb can also mean to vindicate or to acknowledge as right: the crowds “acknowledged God's justice” (Luke 7:29), where the Greek is dikaioō, and no one supposes they made God righteous. That use is one of the plainest signs that the word means ‘declare right’ rather than ‘make righteous’. Jesus also speaks of the last judgment in the same terms, “by your words you will be acquitted” (Matthew 12:37). Luke records Paul's first recorded sermon, in Pisidian Antioch, announcing that “Through Him everyone who believes is justified from everything you could not be justified from by the law of Moses” (Acts 13:39).

Paul's first sustained treatment comes in Galatians, written to churches where teachers were insisting that Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Paul had confronted Peter at Antioch for withdrawing from table fellowship with Gentile Christians, and his account of that confrontation turns into the thesis of the letter: “a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ” (Galatians 2:16). He argues from Abraham, whose faith was credited as righteousness and to whom the gospel was announced in the promise that the nations would be blessed (Galatians 3:6-9), and from the cross: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). If righteousness could come through the law, “Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21). In Galatians justification is inseparable from the question of who belongs at the table; those who share Abraham's faith are Abraham's children, Jew and Gentile together.

Romans sets out the argument at full length. Paul announces that the gospel “reveals the righteousness of God that comes by faith from start to finish” (Romans 1:17), then spends two and a half chapters showing that Gentile and Jew alike stand guilty, concluding that “no one will be justified in His sight by works of the law” (Romans 3:20). Then comes the turn: “But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been revealed” (Romans 3:21). All have sinned and “are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 3:24). God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice “so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26), which is Paul's answer to the problem Exodus 23:7 and Proverbs 17:15 raised: God acquits the ungodly without denying justice because the cross deals with their sin. Romans 4 returns to Abraham, who believed “in Him who justifies the wicked” (Romans 4:5), and to David's blessing on the one whose sin is not counted. Christ “was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification” (Romans 4:25). The fruit is peace: “since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God” (Romans 5:1). Romans 5:12-21 sets Adam and Christ side by side, “through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19), and Romans 8 ends the argument in the courtroom of the last day: “Who will bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies” (Romans 8:33). The same shape appears in 2 Corinthians 5:21, where God “made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God”, and in Philippians 3:9, where Paul wants to be found in Christ, “not having my own righteousness from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ”.

Paul never separates the verdict from a changed life. Justified people have died with Christ and must not go on in sin (Romans 6:1-2); what counts is “faith, expressed through love” (Galatians 5:6); and believers were “washed”, “sanctified”, and “justified” together (1 Corinthians 6:11). Paul also teaches that God “will repay each one according to his deeds” (Romans 2:6) and that “the doers of the law” will be declared righteous (Romans 2:13), texts that interpreters relate to justification by faith in different ways. The later letters keep the same teaching: Titus 3:5-7 says God saved us “not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy”, so that, “having been justified by His grace”, we might become heirs, and Ephesians 2:8-10 says salvation is “not by works, so that no one can boast”, yet we were created “to do good works”.

James 2:14-26 is the text every account must face. James writes, “a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone” (James 2:24), and cites the same Genesis 15:6 Paul cites, pointing to Abraham's offering of Isaac in Genesis 22. Most interpreters, ancient and modern, hold that James and Paul are not answering the same question. Paul is asking on what basis a sinner is accepted by God and excludes works of the law as that basis; James is attacking a claimed faith that produces no deeds, which he calls dead, and uses ‘justified’ of the demonstration that faith is real (James 2:22 says Abraham's faith “was perfected by what he did”). Others hold that James uses ‘justify’ of the final verdict, which takes account of the whole life. Either way, the New Testament holds both that the verdict is a gift received by faith and that the faith that receives it is never alone.

keyTexts.why: Abram believes the promise and it is credited to him as righteousness, before circumcision and before the law. Paul and James both build on this verse.
The judge is to acquit the innocent and condemn the guilty. The courtroom sense of ‘justify’ is established here, and it frames the scandal of God justifying the ungodly.
David blesses the one whose sin the LORD does not count against him. Paul quotes it as the other side of crediting: sin not counted, righteousness counted.
No one alive is righteous before God. Paul echoes the verse in Galatians 2:16 and Romans 3:20.
The righteous Servant will justify many and bear their iniquities. The verdict and the bearing of sin are joined in one sentence.
The righteous will live by faith. Paul quotes it in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11 as a summary of the gospel.
The high priest in filthy garments is defended against the accuser, stripped of his iniquity, and clothed in clean robes. A picture of acquittal as God's own act.
The tax collector who asks only for mercy goes home justified, and the Pharisee who lists his virtues does not. Jesus' own parable of the doctrine.
Justification is by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, and it decides whether Jewish and Gentile believers eat at one table.
The center of Paul's argument. God's righteousness is revealed apart from the law, sinners are justified freely by grace, and the cross shows God to be just and the justifier.
Abraham and David show that God credits righteousness apart from works to the one who trusts him who justifies the ungodly.
The result of justification is peace with God and access into grace. The verdict opens a relationship, not just a file.
No charge can stand against God's elect because God is the one who justifies. The present verdict anticipates the last judgment.
The sinless one was made sin for us so that in him we might become the righteousness of God. A key text in the debate over imputation.
Faith without deeds is dead, and Abraham was justified by what he did. The text that keeps the doctrine from being read as permission for an idle faith.

history:
The earliest Christian writers repeat Paul's language without making it a controversy. Clement of Rome, writing to the church at Corinth around AD 96 (1 Clement 32), says that believers are justified not through their own wisdom, piety, or works but through faith, and in the next chapter urges them not to grow slack in good works. Augustine of Hippo gave the West its framework. In On the Spirit and the Letter (412), written during his controversy with Pelagius, a British monk who taught that human beings can obey God by their natural powers, Augustine argued that justification is wholly God's gracious act, but he understood the Latin iustificare as ‘to make righteous’, God healing the will by pouring his love into the heart (Romans 5:5). The Council of Orange (529) confirmed that grace comes before any good movement of the will. Medieval theology, summed up by Thomas Aquinas in his Summa Theologiae (I-II, question 113), described justification as the forgiveness of sins together with the infusion of grace, a real change in the person. The Eastern churches, meanwhile, spoke of salvation chiefly as union with God and participation in his life, and justification never became a dividing question for them.

The Reformation made it one. Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar and professor at Wittenberg, lectured on Romans in 1515 and 1516; in 1545 he recalled that his breakthrough came when he understood the righteousness of God in Romans 1:17 not as the justice by which God punishes but as the righteousness by which God, in mercy, justifies through faith. Historians date that insight anywhere from about 1513 to 1519. The Augsburg Confession (1530), Article IV, states that people are justified freely for Christ's sake through faith, not by their own merits. John Calvin, in the final edition of his Institutes of the Christian Religion (1559, book 3, chapters 11 to 18), defined justification as God's acceptance of sinners, consisting in the forgiveness of sins and the imputation (the crediting) of Christ's righteousness, and called it the chief hinge of religion. Both Lutheran and Reformed theologians rejected Andreas Osiander's teaching that believers are righteous by the indwelling of Christ's divine righteousness; the Lutheran Formula of Concord (1577), Article III, and Calvin (Institutes 3.11) both answered him. The Thirty-Nine Articles of the Church of England (Article XI) and the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646, chapter 11) state the Protestant position, the latter adding that faith is the only instrument of justification yet is never alone in the justified person.

Rome answered at the Council of Trent. An attempt at agreement at the Colloquy of Regensburg in 1541 produced a compromise article that neither side ratified. Trent's Decree on Justification, adopted in its sixth session on 13 January 1547, taught that justification is not only the forgiveness of sins but also the sanctification and renewal of the inner person; that its single formal cause is the righteousness of God by which he makes us righteous; that faith is the beginning, foundation, and root of justification; and that justifying grace is lost by mortal sin and restored through penance. Its canons condemned the teaching that justifying faith is nothing but confidence in divine mercy. John Wesley, after hearing Luther's preface to Romans read at a meeting in Aldersgate Street, London, on 24 May 1738, taught justification by faith alone together with a strong call to holiness, and the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions have held the Protestant doctrine while rejecting unconditional election.

The twentieth century reopened the question from two sides. Ecumenically, Hans Küng's dissertation Justification (1957) argued that Karl Barth's doctrine and Trent's were compatible, and decades of dialogue led to the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, signed by the Lutheran World Federation and the Roman Catholic Church in Augsburg on 31 October 1999. It states a consensus on basic truths, that we are accepted by God by grace alone through faith in Christ's saving work and not because of any merit on our part, and it declares that the sixteenth-century condemnations do not apply to the teaching each side now presents, while leaving real differences open. The World Methodist Council affirmed it in 2006, the Anglican Consultative Council welcomed it in 2016, and the World Communion of Reformed Churches associated itself with it in 2017. Many confessional Lutherans, Reformed, and evangelicals judged that the declaration papered over the differences. In biblical scholarship, E. P. Sanders's Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977) argued that the Judaism of Paul's day was not a religion of earning salvation but what he called covenantal nomism, grace first and law as the way of staying in; James D. G. Dunn named the resulting approach the New Perspective on Paul in a 1982 lecture published in 1983, and N. T. Wright developed it further. John Piper's The Future of Justification (2007) and Wright's reply, Justification (2009), set out the debate, and John M. G. Barclay's Paul and the Gift (2015) reframed it around the ancient idea of the gift. The site's page on how we are saved surveys these views at length.

differ.body: Justification is a legal verdict, not a process of inner renewal. God forgives the sinner and credits to him the righteousness of Christ, his obedience and his death, so that the believer is accepted as righteous on the ground of what Christ has done and not on the ground of anything worked in him, even by grace. Faith is the empty hand that receives the gift; it is not itself a virtue God rewards. Sanctification, the lifelong renewal of the believer, always follows and is inseparable from justification, but it must never be mixed into it, or the troubled conscience is sent back to its own progress for assurance. Defenders point to Romans 4:5, where God justifies the ungodly, to 2 Corinthians 5:21 and Philippians 3:9, and to the courtroom meaning of dikaioō.

Justification is God's gracious act by which a sinner is not only forgiven but truly made righteous, as God's love is poured into the heart by the Holy Spirit (Romans 5:5). Grace comes first and is entirely unearned, and no one can merit the grace of justification. Faith is the beginning and root of it, and faith is joined with hope and charity, since what counts is “faith, expressed through love” (Galatians 5:6). Because justification is a real transformation, it can grow, it can be lost through grave sin, and it can be restored through repentance and the sacrament of penance; good works done in grace are God's gifts that he graciously rewards. Defenders point to James 2:24, to Paul's teaching on judgment according to deeds, and to Augustine. The Joint Declaration (1999) holds that this view and the Lutheran one share a basic consensus.

The Orthodox churches confess that salvation is entirely God's gift in Christ, but they do not make the courtroom the governing picture. The goal of salvation is theosis, union with God and participation in his life by grace, as 2 Peter 1:4 speaks of sharing in the divine nature. Justification is one real biblical image among many, and it is not separated from healing, illumination, and the believer's life in the church and its sacraments. The Orthodox generally regard the Western quarrel of the sixteenth century as built on Western assumptions they never shared, such as sharp distinctions between declaring and making righteous, and they read Paul through the Greek fathers, especially the teaching of Athanasius and others that the Son became man so that humanity might share in God.

Scholars such as James Dunn and N. T. Wright argue that the Reformation read Paul through Luther's struggle with medieval penance, and that Paul's actual opponents were not trying to earn salvation. By ‘works of the law’ Paul chiefly meant the practices that marked Jews off from Gentiles, such as circumcision, food laws, and the sabbath. Justification is God's declaration of who belongs to his one covenant family, the people of Abraham now made up of Jews and Gentiles through faith in the Messiah, and so it is both a verdict about sin and a verdict about membership. Wright stresses the future justification at the last judgment, which will accord with the whole life lived by the Spirit. Its defenders hold that this recovers the social and missionary heart of Galatians and Romans; its critics, including Stephen Westerholm and John Piper, argue that it weakens Paul's teaching on grace against human achievement and on the imputed righteousness of Christ.

errors:
The church has rejected two opposite distortions, and Paul answered both. The first is that a person can stand before God on his own record, whether by moral effort, religious observance, or a mixture of grace and merit in which God supplies the first part and we supply the rest. Pelagius's teaching was condemned for this reason at the Council of Carthage in 418, and Paul's word against the teachers in Galatia is that if righteousness could come through the law, Christ died for nothing (Galatians 2:21). Every tradition in the section above rejects it; the Council of Trent itself condemned the idea that a person can be justified by his own works done apart from divine grace. The second distortion is the reverse: that because the verdict is free, the life does not matter. Paul anticipated the question, “Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase?” (Romans 6:1), and refused it, and James calls a faith without deeds dead. Dietrich Bonhoeffer's Discipleship (1937) named this cheap grace, the forgiveness proclaimed without repentance or obedience.

Other errors are subtler. Faith can be treated as a work, a mental effort that earns acceptance, when Scripture treats it as trust that looks away from itself to Christ. Justification can be cut off from Christ himself, as if it were a transaction apart from the person of the Savior, when Paul speaks of seeking “to be justified in Christ” (Galatians 2:17). And each side of the Reformation divide has often caricatured the other, Protestants accusing Catholics of teaching salvation by works and Catholics accusing Protestants of teaching that holiness is unnecessary. Both caricatures have been rejected by the traditions they describe, whatever real differences remain.
life:
Justification settles where a person stands with God, and it settles it from outside the person. That is its first gift to ordinary life. A conscience that keeps its own accounts is never at rest, because the books never balance and the audit never ends. The believer's confidence before God rests on God's verdict about Christ, not on a daily reading of spiritual progress, and so Paul can say that the result is peace (Romans 5:1). This does not make repentance unnecessary; it makes repentance possible, because a person who knows he is accepted can afford to tell the truth about his sin.

The doctrine also reshapes how people treat one another. Because the verdict comes by grace, boasting is excluded (Romans 3:27), and the ground is level: the tax collector and the Pharisee, the Jew and the Gentile, the lifelong churchgoer and the latecomer stand on the same footing. Paul first argued the doctrine to keep Jewish and Gentile believers eating at one table. People who have been acquitted have little ground for condemning others, and every reason to extend the mercy they received. And because the verdict of the last day has already been spoken over those in Christ, they can face death, failure, and accusation, whether from others, from conscience, or from the accuser himself, with the question of Romans 8:33 in their mouths.
questions: Exodus 23:7 and Proverbs 17:15 say God does not acquit the guilty, yet Romans 4:5 says he justifies the wicked. How does Romans 3:21-26 answer that tension?
Paul and James both quote Genesis 15:6 and seem to reach opposite conclusions. What question is each of them answering, and how do their answers fit together?
In Galatians, justification decided who could share a table. Where might the doctrine challenge the walls between Christians, or between you and someone else, today?
